## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}

In past, people live in huts in a hamlet but as space becomes a constraint, stacking houses vertically becomes an economic solution. The direct implication is that instead of having address for say ten homes, now you have the address of the building and the floor number.

A vector in programming is essentially an higher level object that store sequence of object *of the same type*. To access any specific value, you just need to know the name of the building and the floor number.

This analogy only works when each floor which called entry are of the same type (all numbers, all logical, or all strings). If the entry is homogenous, a list is used @sec-list. This is also where  indexing must be a discrete number/integer @sec-discrete_continuous and @sec-numeric.

The key point is that a vector is a "new type" of object constructed by a sequence of atomic object. It has similar structure: variable name, assignment, and value. One can retrieve the values based on the order they appear in the list.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
To construct a vector in R we use the function, `c()` short for concatenate.

`vector_name <- c(object1, object2,..., objectn)`

- Length of a vector is the number of elements in the vector i.

- To access the p-th element of that vector, one uses the square bracket symbol "[]", so `vector_name[2]` will return object2. The order is also called index and should be an integer.

- In R you can use negative index, which delete the entry.  Vector_name[-2] will remove object2 from the output.

- It is also possible to It is possible to access the element without using their order. See in the example below, this can under specific scenarios, e.g., short vector as you need to give a specific name to each ordered element or you don't want to remember the name. This is called giving names/attributes to eache element.


## Examples {.unnumbered}

- Contructing a vector
```{r}

# create
c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)

c(2L, 1L, 4L)

c("Hello", "world")

test <- c("Hello", "world")

paste(test)
```



- Accessing single values
```{r}
# access
test[1]

test[2]
```

- Accessing multiple index by using `vector of integer`

```{r}
# a vector of vector

test[c(1, 2)]
test[c(2, 1)]
```


- Constructing from more vectors

```{r}
c(test, 1)

vec1 <- c(1, 4, 5)
vec2 <- c(10, 11, 12)

vec_combined <- c(vec1, vec2)
```

- Deleting one or more element.

```{r}
# remove the first element
vec_combined[-1]

# remove the first and fourth element
vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]

vec_combined # unchanged
```

One can construct a new vector by

```{r}
sub_vector <- vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]
sub_vector
```

One can also use the same but remember you cannot retrieve the old one (think about saving a file using the same filename)

```{r}
vec_combined <- vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]
vec_combined
```


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Semantic: entry, element, values

- Concatenation priority
 - Boolean to integer

```{r}
#| echo: true

str(c(TRUE, FALSE, 4L))
```

- Integer to numeric

```{r}
#| echo: true

str(c(TRUE, FALSE, 4))

str(c(1L, 2L, 4))
```
 - Numeric to character

```{r}
#| echo: true

str(c(TRUE, TRUE, "text"))

str(c(TRUE, 1.2, "text"))
```

- Atomic elements are considered as vector in R. The [1] means R displays the first element

```{r}
#| echo: true

a <- 1
a
```
- when you print many elements, you will see [1] [38] etc on the left side of the output. It is displaying index so the one on the right is simply. Note that it depends on the size of your console, so a narrow vs wide one.

```{r}
rpois(300, 4)

```

- A vector has a length l, if you try to access vector_name[n] where n is bigger than n, it will return NA.
- In R, you can actually use numeric, so vector_name[1.2] is the same as vector_name[1]. It is hard-cored in R, that it will automatical round the number to the lowest integer. In some cases, it is quite practical, in other it might be problematic.
- A more tedious way of constructing a vector where you can call by the name and not the index

```{r}
#| echo: true
room <- c(width = 15, height = 12)
attributes(room)

room["width"]
```
